title: The Crown
part: PART THREE: WHAT THE MOUNTAIN KNEW

pages.text:
*From the Walk-Book of Highstep, Day 21. Weather: clear, and very large. Distance: three miles. Direction: left. Mo is up the mountain. So is the goat.*

The pines stopped dead.

Then came the bare grey stone, shimmering in the moonlight. It was warm under Mo’s bare feet, not the cold chill of rock, but a deep, living heat. He pressed his heel into the stone, testing it. The pulse was there, slow and steady. It felt like resting on a sleeping dog’s flank, where the breath rises in a heavy sigh.

Admiral followed close. His hooves clicked on the hard surface. The goat did not complain about the heat. He did not complain about the dark. He simply moved with a purpose that Mo had learned to respect, his tin bell silent in the cold air.

Mo climbed over a ridge of wind-flattened grass. The blades brushed his shins. Then he faced the final ascent to the Crown. The air smelled of pine resin and cold stone, a sharp, clean scent that made his head ache in a good way.

He took a breath. He filled his lungs.

Then he climbed.
pages.image: A small barefoot boy in a green poncho climbs a slope of warm grey stone under a starry sky, followed by a large brown and white goat with a tin bell, their breath visible in the cold night air.

pages.text:
The Crown was not a peak in the way a mountain peak should be. It was a hollow, a shallow basin of rock that held the wind and the stars. Mo stood in the center of it, his feet spread wide, feeling the full weight of the world above him. The night was immense, a dome of black velvet studded with diamonds so bright they seemed to burn. There was no horizon, only a curve of sky that went on forever.

He looked down. The village was a speck of light in the distance, a cluster of lanterns clinging to the side of the mountain. He could not see the people, but he could feel them, a faint vibration in the air, a hum of life that connected him to every soul in Highstep. Admiral lay down at his feet, tucking his nose under his tail. The goat was warm, a solid mass of brown and white fur that radiated heat into Mo’s cold ankles. Mo leaned back against a stone, closing his eyes. He did not feel afraid. He felt watched.
pages.image: A small boy and a large goat sit in a hollow of grey rock on a mountain top, surrounded by a vast, star-filled night sky, with a tiny village visible far below in the darkness.

pages.text:
Mo blinked, certain he had fallen asleep on the cold rock and dreamed this. A single golden point of light burned low in the eastern dark, steady as a candle in a window, though there were no windows out here. It did not twinkle like a star; it moved, sliding across the blackness with the slow, deliberate grace of a heavy cart rolling over cobblestones.

He rubbed his eyes with his sleeves and looked again. The light was still there. Then a second glow appeared to the north, and a third to the west. They were not stars at all. They were lanterns. Or rather, they were villages, distant clusters of warm light clinging to the backs of other walking mountains, just like Highstep. Mo counted them carefully, his breath misting in the cold air. One, two, three. They were drifting closer, drawn by some quiet force he could not see but could feel humming in the deep bones of the earth beneath his bare feet.
pages.image: A boy stands on a rocky outcrop at night, looking out at a dark horizon where several small, glowing lights move slowly across the landscape like distant lanterns.

pages.text:
The hum changed pitch.

It stopped being just a rumble in the moss and climbed up, a deep, resonant note that vibrated in Mo’s ribs and settled hard in his teeth. It was a song, ancient and sad, waiting a thousand years to be sung.

Then the dark answered.

Seven notes, clear and bright, wove together into a chord so pure Mo’s eyes stung. It sounded like a family calling across a long distance. A greeting. Coming home.

Mo stood still. His bare feet pressed into the warm rock, grounding him against the wind. He felt the mountain’s pulse beneath him, steady as a drum in a schoolyard.

He didn’t need to understand it.

He didn’t need to believe it.

He just needed to hear it. The sound filled the hollow, then his chest, until he was certain he was not alone. He had never been alone.
pages.image: A boy stands with his eyes closed on a mountain top, his hands pressed against his chest, as a faint, golden glow surrounds him in the dark, representing a deep, resonant hum he feels in his bones.

pages.text:
A tear rolled down Mo’s cheek, and he did not bother to wipe it away. It was not a sad tear. It was a tear of relief, of wonder, of a truth that had finally found its way to the surface. He grinned, a wide, sharp smile that showed his teeth. If Highstep could not believe a barefoot boy, they could believe their own eyes. They could see the lights. They could hear the song.

He kicked Admiral awake. The goat blinked, shook his head, and stood up, his tin bell jingling softly. Mo took the lantern from his poncho and lit it. The flame was small, but it was enough. It was enough to see the path down. It was enough to show them the way. He turned and began to climb down, his bare feet finding the stone, step by step, guided by the mountain that loved him.
pages.image: A small boy in a green poncho holds a lit lantern, climbing down a dark rocky slope with a large goat following closely behind, their faces illuminated by the warm light in the night.
